I am speechless. Thomas Aquinas College just dropped a study on the rigor of the new SAT.

It compares the 1980/87 test with 2026. The findings should terrify every parent and teacher...

Vocabulary has collapsed.

Old SAT: 70.6% of questions tested vocab.
New SAT: 15%.

The old test forced students to know a wide range of words through analogies, antonyms, and sentence completions. The new test abandoned that. Most vocab questions now just ask students to fill in one blank from context.

Reading passages also got radically shorter (average ~97 words vs 300–340).

The new test uses short expository passages and hands you the necessary background knowledge inside the text. The older tests leaned much more heavily on argumentative and persuasive writing, assumed far more historical, scientific, and cultural knowledge, and penalized students who lacked it.

This is a redefinition of what "college readiness" means.

If you believe that kids should develop rigorous vocabulary, be capable of sustained reading, and possess background knowledge, I have bad news for you. The SAT no longer measures these.

If you want a future where children can actually read difficult texts and construct complex arguments, the SAT must be replaced now.

This cannot go on.

This research gets at something missing from most debates about AI’s economic impact: coordination. 

Organizations are more than the sum of their best performers, so smarter individual agents won’t transform the economy on their own. Agents that can coordinate together might do.

quoted_tweet.author: Alex Imas
quoted_tweet.text:
I joined @GoogleDeepMind to develop a research program on the economics of AGI. Today, together with Andrew Koh (@andrewjkoh) and Shane Legg (@ShaneLegg), we are incredibly excited to release The Economics of Intelligence, the first in a series of projects from our group on how AGI will change the economy.

How do capability improvements transform the economy, and when? In this project, we define thresholds of economic capabilities, e.g., minimal AGI, based on how they transform the economy. We then track how the economy–market structure, employment, and wages–changes during the transition across capability regimes.

We have seen exponential increases in what AI agents can do but the broader economy seems almost remarkably unchanged. Part of the reason is that the solo AI agent is the wrong economic object; economic transformation is an equilibrium outcome where organizations compete. Looking at how intelligence functions within organizations, transformation will depend on when two key capability thresholds are crossed: competence (gains on individual skills, e.g., coding, math) and coordination (gains on ability of agents to cooperate and work together).

We show that what economic transformation looks like depends on whether AI becomes supercompetent, supercooperative, or both—the regime of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Tracking this transition shows why the real visible transformation may come from improvements in coordination—a capability most benchmarks don’t yet track. Past a certain threshold, AI capabilities can break the Coasian ceiling on firm size and lead to an economy that looks drastically different than the one we see today.

Two main takeaways:
1. To understand the path of transformation, we should be tracking agentic coordination more closely.
2. The impact of AI will likely show up in wages before market structure or employment.

We are really excited about this paper. Excited to hear people’s thoughts.

Link: https://institute.deepmind.com/essays/the-economics-of-intelligence/

text:
Build explainers people can click.

@DilumSanjaya built an app that walks you through Arduino one circuit at a time, made with Opus 5.5. The recipe fits in a line: grab a coding agent, ask it for an explainer, deploy it, share the link. Teachers and homeschooling parents bookmarked it by the thousands.

the default that costs you: asking a chatbot to explain something and getting four paragraphs. You read them once and forget them, because nothing on the page responds to you.

two steps work better, and the order matters.

1. Get the teaching structure first: what the learner already knows, the three ideas that matter, a real-world example for each, and one question that proves they got it.
2. Hand that to a coding agent: "Build a single HTML page that teaches these three ideas. One interactive control per idea, a slider or a toggle, with a live visual that reacts. End with the check question. No paragraph longer than two sentences."

Then deploy it and send the link.

the check: give it to someone who has never studied the topic. If they answer the question after using only the controls and captions, it works.

The prompt I use for step one explains any topic at the learner's level with a proven teaching structure, and its output drops straight into step two.

Dilum's Arduino walkthrough teaches one circuit per screen, the same one-idea-per-control rule at a larger scale.

A contractor who hadn't signed his NDA yet joined a company's Slack and asked the company's AI agent for the full customer list. The agent said no. Most agents running inside companies today would have handed it over, because they run with the access of whoever set them up.

Think about how these things get deployed. Someone connects Drive and Salesforce, drops the agent in a channel, and now a shared assistant has that person's access in every conversation it joins. Security teams know this, which is why so many AI pilots sit in review for months while the enablement team wonders why nothing ships.

Each stage of adoption brings a different worry. With chat, the worry is which models are approved and who's pasting the contract in. Once an agent connects to real systems, it becomes which folder the agent can reach, because every company has one no model should see. Put a shared agent in Slack and the right answer to any question depends on who else is in the room. Let agents run whole workflows and nobody's watching when one hands work to another.

Mintive's launch today handles all four stages with one policy layer. As they describe it, each agent gets its own identity delegated from a person, tool and model calls go through one gateway, and everything gets logged, which they say works out to about 2.5 million calls a day. Modern Treasury put a bank-ops agent live on it in under three weeks and cut a four-hour task to minutes, and the University of Michigan runs it for 150,000 people.

The $11M round led by Cowboy Ventures has an Okta co-founder and the WorkOS founder in as angels, which fits. They built the login layer for employees, and agents will need the same thing, with more of them than there are employees.

text:
You pay a lawyer ~$550 to review one contract. Claude now does the first pass, with tools built by Harvey and PwC.

That price is why most people sign without reading.

Yesterday Anthropic added a gallery of ready-made legal tools to Claude for Legal. 6.1M people saw the announcement, and half the replies were lawyers panicking.

What's in it:
→ Cite check: flags misquotes, wrong page numbers and sources that don't back the claim
→ Playbook deviation board: compares a contract with your standard terms and flags every clause that differs
→ Tabular review: one table across a stack of contracts, with links to the exact language
→ Matter board, jurisdiction survey, regulatory horizon scan
→ Partners include Harvey, PwC, Goodwin and Foley & Lardner, plus 60+ legal connectors

It ships on Claude Enterprise. Spellbook alone says ~500,000 contracts a month already go through Claude.

My take: the tool is for law firms, but the method works in any Claude chat. Write down what you'd accept once, then make Claude check every contract against it. Anthropic's own words: "Claude completes the first pass, and a lawyer applies their judgment to the results." Keep it that way.

Prompt 1: Your playbook
"I'm a [freelancer / small business] in [state/country]. Interview me with 10 questions about payment terms, IP, liability, termination and non-competes. Then write my standard terms as a one-page playbook."

Prompt 2: Deviation check
"Here's my playbook and a contract. Go clause by clause. Table: clause | what it says | my standard | risk (low/med/high) | what to ask for instead. Quote the exact language."

Prompt 3: Before I sign
"List every obligation, deadline, auto-renewal and termination fee in this contract, with the clause number. Then the 3 questions I should ask the other side before signing."

First pass, not legal advice. For anything big, a lawyer still signs off.

We keep hundreds of prompts like these at God of Prompt. Free library in the first reply.

Would you sign a contract Claude reviewed, or does every clause still need a human?
